content: Recognizing the utility of antenatal care (ANC) as a platform for critical healthcare functions, including health promotion and disease prevention, the World Health Organization (WHO) 2016 ANC guidelines included 14 out of 49 recommendations specifically addressing nutritional interventions during pregnancy. In April 2019, in light of emerging evidence, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized updating the recommendation on vitamin D supplementation. This updated recommendation builds upon, but does not alter, the original guidance on vitamin D supplementation provided in the 2016 WHO ANC guidelines. Pregnancy necessitates a balanced diet that meets the increased energy, protein, vitamin, and mineral requirements of both the mother and the developing fetus. Vitamin D, a fat-soluble vitamin, is primarily synthesized in the human body through sunlight exposure but can also be obtained from dietary sources such as fish-liver oils, fatty fish, mushrooms, egg yolks, and liver. Vitamin D plays a crucial role in maintaining normal blood levels of calcium and phosphate, which are essential for general cellular function and, more specifically, for bone health. Quantifying daily vitamin D intake is challenging due to the lack of precise food composition data and the numerous factors influencing skin synthesis. These factors include darker skin pigmentation, limited sunlight exposure, living at latitudes above 40 degrees, colder seasons, older age, and sunscreen use. Fetuses acquire vitamin D from their mothers, and this maternal supply serves as the primary source of vitamin D for infants during the first few months of life, particularly for those who are breastfed. Vitamin D deficiency is a global issue, with a notably high prevalence among pregnant women in Middle Eastern and Asian countries. During pregnancy, vitamin D deficiency has been associated with adverse outcomes such as pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), preterm birth, and low birth weight. In 2016, the WHO ANC Guideline Development Group (GDG) reviewed evidence on the effects of vitamin D deficiency, as well as considerations related to values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. At that time, the evidence was deemed insufficient to recommend routine vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy. However, since the publication of the 2016 guidelines, the Cochrane review on vitamin D supplementation in pregnancy has been updated to include additional trials. This updated evidence, as of July 12, 2018, has been incorporated into the framework for evaluating the effects and considerations relevant to vitamin D supplementation in routine ANC. The updated recommendation aligns with WHO's commitment to evidence-informed policies and practices, as well as its living guidelines approach. The Departments of Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH), Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA), and Nutrition and Food Safety (NFS) prioritized this update following the identification of new evidence on vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy. The target audience for this guideline includes national and local public health policymakers, program managers, healthcare professionals (e.g., obstetricians, midwives, nurses, and general practitioners), and academic staff involved in training the health workforce. The recommendation is relevant to all pregnant women and adolescent girls receiving ANC in any healthcare or community-based setting, as well as their unborn fetuses and newborns. The updated recommendation was developed using WHO's standardized guideline development procedures, which include identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for implementation and evaluation. The process was overseen by the Executive GSG, an independent panel of external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions. This group advised on prioritizing new and existing questions in maternal and perinatal health for guideline development or updating. The WHO Steering Group, comprising staff from the SRH, MCA, and NFS departments, managed the updating process. They drafted the key recommendation question in PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format and identified individuals to participate as guideline methodologists and members of the guideline development and external review groups. The Steering Group also supervised evidence retrieval and synthesis, organized technical consultations, and finalized the guideline document. The Guideline Development Group (GDG), consisting of 15 external experts and stakeholders, appraised the evidence, advised on its interpretation, and formulated the final recommendation during an online meeting in December 2019. The GDG ensured geographic representation, gender balance, and the absence of significant conflicts of interest. The External Review Group (ERG), a geographically and gender-balanced group of five members, peer-reviewed the preliminary guideline document to identify factual errors and provide feedback on clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. Evidence supporting this recommendation was derived from an updated Cochrane systematic review on the effectiveness of antenatal oral vitamin D supplements. The review included randomized controlled trial (RCT) data assessed and synthesized using standardized Cochrane methodology. Additional analyses were conducted to address GDG-specified subgroup analyses and outcomes relevant to the ANC guideline. The updated recommendation reflects the latest evidence and considerations, ensuring that it aligns with the overarching principle of providing a positive pregnancy experience, as defined by maintaining physical and sociocultural normality, ensuring a healthy pregnancy and baby, facilitating a smooth transition to labor and birth, and achieving positive motherhood outcomes.
